questions.visual_target: the complete isolated neonatal chest radiograph
questions.explanation: Mild hyperinflation, perihilar interstitial prominence, and fissural fluid in an otherwise term newborn support transient tachypnea from delayed fetal-lung-fluid clearance.
visual_clues: The lungs are mildly hyperinflated rather than low volume
Perihilar interstitial markings are prominent
Fluid is visible along a fissure
choice_rationales: Correct: Transient tachypnea typically produces mild hyperinflation, perihilar streaking, and fissural fluid from delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid.
Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome produces low lung volumes with diffuse fine granular opacity and air bronchograms, unlike this hyperinflated interstitial pattern.
Meconium aspiration usually produces coarse, patchy, asymmetric air-space opacities with marked hyperinflation and possible air leak.
Neonatal pneumonia may cause focal or diffuse air-space opacity but is less specifically associated with the combination of fissural fluid and rapid postnatal improvement.
questions.ground_truth_evidence: The local teaching composite identifies transient tachypnea of the newborn and duplicates the same neonatal radiograph with an annotation over the right minor fissure. The quiz variant preserves the complete unannotated left radiograph while excluding the answer title and redundant annotated duplicate.

questions.stem: Which named CT sign is demonstrated by the enhancing pleural layers surrounding this lentiform collection?
questions.case_context: A patient with persistent fever after bacterial pneumonia has pleuritic pain and a loculated pleural collection.
questions.visual_target: the complete axial contrast-enhanced CT image, especially the outlined pleural collection
options: Extrapleural sign of a chest-wall mass
questions.explanation: Enhancement and separation of the visceral and parietal pleura around infected pleural fluid is the split pleura sign, a characteristic CT feature of empyema.
visual_clues: A lentiform collection is centered in the pleural space
Enhancing visceral and parietal pleural layers are separated by fluid
Adjacent lung is compressed medially
choice_rationales: Correct: The split pleura sign consists of enhancing visceral and parietal pleural layers separated by a pleural collection, exactly as shown here.
The comet-tail sign is a curving bundle of bronchovascular structures entering a pleural-based rounded opacity, not two enhancing pleural layers around fluid.
The deep sulcus sign is an abnormally lucent and deep costophrenic angle on a supine chest radiograph, not this contrast-enhanced CT appearance.
The extrapleural sign is a smoothly tapered intrathoracic opacity with displaced extrapleural fat, not a fluid collection splitting the pleural layers.
questions.ground_truth_evidence: The local teaching image identifies the split pleura sign. The complete contrast-enhanced axial CT demonstrates a lentiform pleural collection bounded by enhancing visceral and parietal pleural layers, the characteristic CT sign of empyema.

questions.stem: Which named chest-radiograph sign is illustrated by the abnormal panel and its magnified comparison?
questions.case_context: A patient develops acute pleuritic chest pain and unexplained hypoxemia after prolonged immobilization.
questions.visual_target: both comparison radiographs and their magnified vascular regions, interpreted together
questions.explanation: Abrupt pulmonary-artery cutoff with decreased distal vascular markings produces the Westermark sign of pulmonary embolism.
visual_clues: There is abrupt pulmonary-artery cutoff
Vascular markings are decreased distal to the cutoff
The paired normal panel emphasizes focal regional oligemia
choice_rationales: Correct: Westermark sign is focal pulmonary oligemia distal to embolic obstruction, represented here by abrupt arterial cutoff and decreased peripheral vascular markings.
Hampton hump is a peripheral pleural-based wedge-shaped opacity from pulmonary infarction rather than regional vascular pruning.
Fleischner sign is enlargement of a central pulmonary artery, not the distal oligemia emphasized in this comparison.
Golden S sign is deformation of the minor fissure by right-upper-lobe collapse around a central mass, not pulmonary vascular cutoff.
questions.ground_truth_evidence: The local teaching composite identifies the Westermark sign and demonstrates it by comparing a normal chest radiograph with pulmonary-embolism-associated abrupt pulmonary-artery cutoff and decreased distal vascular markings. questions.stem: Which interstitial-lung-disease pattern is best demonstrated on this axial HRCT image?
questions.case_context: A patient with a connective-tissue disease has progressive exertional dyspnea and a restrictive pulmonary-function pattern.
questions.visual_target: the complete axial HRCT image, especially the peripheral lower-lung pattern
questions.explanation: Symmetric basal ground-glass opacity and fine reticulation with traction bronchiectasis and relative subpleural sparing favor an NSIP pattern.
visual_clues: Ground-glass opacity and fine reticulation are bilateral and symmetric
A thin immediate subpleural rim is relatively spared
Traction bronchiectatic change is present without dominant stacked honeycombing
choice_rationales: Correct: NSIP commonly produces symmetric lower-lung ground-glass opacity and fine reticulation with traction bronchiectasis and relative subpleural sparing.
UIP is more heterogeneous and subpleural, with basal stacked honeycombing and little relative subpleural sparing.
Fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis more often combines fibrosis with mosaic attenuation, air trapping, centrilobular nodules, or a three-density pattern.
Organizing pneumonia usually produces patchy peripheral or peribronchovascular consolidation rather than this symmetric fine fibrotic interstitial pattern.
questions.ground_truth_evidence: The local teaching image identifies nonspecific interstitial pneumonia. The complete axial HRCT displays the characteristic combination of bilateral ground-glass opacity, fine reticulation, traction bronchiectatic change, and relative immediate subpleural sparing.

questions.stem: Which named CT pattern is demonstrated by the branching peripheral opacities and their nodular tips?
questions.case_context: A patient with chronic cough has bronchiectasis and a chronic small-airway infection.
questions.visual_target: the axial CT and its magnified small-airway inset, interpreted together
questions.explanation: Branching centrilobular opacities ending in small nodules form the tree-in-bud pattern, which reflects material within and around terminal bronchioles.
visual_clues: Small nodules are centered at the ends of branching linear opacities
The branching structures occupy the peripheral small-airway distribution
The magnified inset shows a budding-tree configuration
choice_rationales: Correct: Tree-in-bud describes centrilobular branching opacities with nodular tips caused by impacted or inflamed small airways, matching the magnified pattern.
Crazy paving combines ground-glass opacity with superimposed interlobular and intralobular septal lines rather than nodular branching bronchioles.
Honeycombing consists of stacked subpleural cystic air spaces and architectural distortion, not fine branching nodules.
Miliary disease produces innumerable randomly distributed tiny nodules without the branching airway-centered configuration shown here.

questions.stem: Which opportunistic pulmonary infection is demonstrated by these paired H&E and silver-stained sections?
questions.case_context: An immunocompromised patient has fever, progressive dyspnea, nonproductive cough, and diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacity.
questions.visual_target: both histology panels jointly: H&E on the left and silver stain on the right
questions.explanation: Foamy intra-alveolar exudate on H&E with crescentic cysts highlighted by silver stain is characteristic of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.
visual_clues: Alveoli contain pale foamy eosinophilic material on H&E
Silver stain highlights numerous small dark cyst forms
Many organisms have a crescentic or cup-shaped contour
choice_rationales: Correct: Pneumocystis produces a foamy intra-alveolar exudate, and silver stains reveal numerous round-to-crescentic cyst forms, matching both panels.
Histoplasma appears as tiny narrow-budding yeasts, often within macrophages, rather than diffuse foamy alveolar exudate with cup-shaped cysts.
Cryptococcus is an encapsulated narrow-budding yeast with a prominent clear halo or mucicarmine-positive capsule, not this paired appearance.
Invasive aspergillosis shows septate hyphae with acute-angle branching and tissue invasion rather than numerous small crescentic alveolar cysts.
questions.ground_truth_evidence: The local teaching composite identifies Pneumocystis jirovecii and shows its paired histologic appearances: foamy eosinophilic intra-alveolar material on H&E and dark crescentic cyst forms on Grocott methenamine silver stain. questions.stem: Which deep neck-space infection is represented by the highlighted collection?
questions.case_context: A young child has fever, neck stiffness, drooling, and painful swallowing after an upper-respiratory infection.
questions.visual_target: the complete sagittal upper-airway diagram, especially the highlighted space posterior to the pharynx
questions.explanation: A collection between the posterior pharyngeal wall and the prevertebral tissues occupies the retropharyngeal space and represents a retropharyngeal abscess.
visual_clues: The collection is posterior to the pharynx
It lies anterior to the cervical vertebral bodies
The expanded deep neck space narrows the upper airway
choice_rationales: Correct: A retropharyngeal abscess forms in the deep space immediately posterior to the pharynx and anterior to the cervical spine, matching the highlighted collection.
A peritonsillar abscess is centered lateral to the palatine tonsil in the oropharynx and displaces the uvula, not the posterior pharyngeal wall.
Epiglottitis causes swelling of the epiglottis and supraglottic tissues rather than a discrete posterior deep-neck-space collection.
A laryngocele is an air- or fluid-filled dilation of the laryngeal saccule that extends beside the larynx, not behind the pharynx.
questions.ground_truth_evidence: The local sagittal teaching diagram identifies a retropharyngeal abscess. The quiz variant removes the answer title and diagnosis label while preserving the complete upper-airway anatomy, the highlighted collection, and the non-answer anatomic labels.

questions.stem: Which syndrome is represented by the intrathoracic obstruction and upper-body venous findings shown?
questions.case_context: A patient with a central lung malignancy develops progressive facial swelling and dyspnea.
questions.visual_target: both parts of the complete diagram together: the thoracic obstruction and upper-body venous findings
questions.explanation: Obstruction of superior vena caval flow causes venous hypertension in the head, neck, upper chest, and arms, producing the pattern shown.
visual_clues: An intrathoracic mass compresses a central upper-body vein
Edema and rubor involve the face, neck, and upper chest
Arm veins fail to empty when elevated
choice_rationales: Correct: Superior vena cava obstruction produces facial and upper-extremity venous congestion with distended veins that do not empty on arm elevation, matching the diagram.
Thoracic outlet syndrome usually affects one upper extremity through focal neurovascular compression and does not cause symmetric facial and neck edema.
Constrictive pericarditis causes systemic venous congestion with elevated jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly, and edema rather than isolated upper-body obstruction by a thoracic mass.
Budd-Chiari syndrome obstructs hepatic venous outflow and presents with hepatomegaly, abdominal pain, and ascites, not facial and arm venous congestion.
questions.ground_truth_evidence: The local teaching diagram depicts an intrathoracic mass obstructing central upper-body venous drainage together with facial, neck, and upper-chest edema and failure of arm veins to empty on elevation, the characteristic clinical pattern of superior vena cava syndrome.

questions.stem: Which traumatic pleural diagnosis best unifies the radiographic and CT findings?
questions.case_context: A supine patient is imaged immediately after significant thoracic trauma.
questions.visual_target: both complete panels jointly: the supine chest radiograph and axial CT
questions.explanation: After thoracic trauma, diffuse unilateral opacity on a supine radiograph with hyperattenuating pleural fluid on CT indicates hemothorax.
visual_clues: The supine radiograph shows diffuse unilateral hazy hemithoracic opacity
CT localizes the abnormality to the pleural space
The pleural fluid is hyperattenuating, supporting acute blood
choice_rationales: Correct: Acute blood is hyperattenuating on CT and can layer posteriorly in a supine patient, producing diffuse unilateral hazy opacity on radiography.
A simple serous pleural effusion is lower attenuation on CT and lacks the trauma-linked hyperdense appearance shown here.
Pulmonary contusion is an intraparenchymal patchy ground-glass or consolidative opacity rather than a hyperattenuating pleural collection.
Tension pneumothorax produces pleural air, absent peripheral lung markings, and mass effect rather than pleural fluid and increased hemithoracic opacity.

questions.stem: Identify the neonatal pulmonary disorder shown on this AP chest radiograph.
questions.case_context: An intubated premature newborn has persistent oxygen dependence and chronic respiratory difficulty after prolonged ventilatory support.
questions.visual_target: the complete AP chest radiograph, including both lung fields and all visible support devices
questions.explanation: The diffuse mixture of coarse reticular opacities and small rounded lucencies produces the classic heterogeneous, sponge-like radiographic pattern of bronchopulmonary dysplasia. The endotracheal tube, enteric tube, and central venous catheter are appropriately positioned. Patient rotation to the left elongates the projected left ribs and shifts the cardiomediastinal silhouette leftward on the image.
visual_clues: Coarse ill-defined reticular markings are diffuse in both lungs
Small rounded lucent areas are interspersed throughout the abnormal lung
The heterogeneous reticulocystic pattern is present in an intubated newborn
choice_rationales: Correct: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia produces chronic coarse bilateral reticular opacity with scattered small lucent or cystic areas, matching the diffuse heterogeneous pattern in this intubated newborn.

Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome more typically shows low-volume lungs with fine, uniform granular or ground-glass opacity and air bronchograms, not this coarse mixed reticular-and-lucent pattern.

Pulmonary interstitial emphysema produces branching or tubular interstitial air lucencies that often radiate from the hilum and may be asymmetric, rather than the diffuse chronic coarse reticulocystic pattern shown here.

Meconium aspiration usually causes patchy, asymmetric air-space opacities with marked hyperinflation and possible air leaks, not the evenly diffuse coarse reticular markings with many small rounded lucencies seen here.

questions.explanation: Visible intercellular bridges indicate squamous differentiation and support squamous cell carcinoma.
visual_clues: Adjacent polygonal cells remain connected by fine intercellular bridges
The cells have more cytoplasm than small-cell carcinoma
No malignant glands or organoid neuroendocrine nests dominate
choice_rationales: Correct: fine bridges between adjacent atypical polygonal cells are a classic feature of squamous differentiation.
Adenocarcinoma would show malignant gland formation or mucin rather than conspicuous intercellular bridges.
Small cell carcinoma has small hyperchromatic cells with scant cytoplasm and nuclear molding, not polygonal cells joined by bridges.
A carcinoid tumor usually forms uniform organoid nests or trabeculae with salt-and-pepper chromatin, which are absent here.

questions.tested_concept: Haller index measurement for pectus excavatum
questions.stem: Identify the thoracic measurement demonstrated on this CT image.
options: Haller index measurement for pectus excavatum
questions.explanation: The ratio of internal transverse diameter to minimum anteroposterior diameter on axial CT is the Haller index used to quantify pectus excavatum.
visual_clues: The image is an axial chest CT through a depressed sternum
One line measures the internal transverse chest diameter
A perpendicular line measures the shortest sternum-to-spine distance
choice_rationales: Correct: the Haller index divides the internal transverse chest diameter by the shortest sternum-to-spine distance on axial CT.
The cardiothoracic ratio compares cardiac width with thoracic width on a frontal chest radiograph, not two perpendicular CT chest dimensions.
The Cobb angle measures spinal curvature on a coronal radiograph and does not use transverse and AP chest diameters.
The pulmonary artery-to-aorta ratio compares vascular diameters near the pulmonary-artery bifurcation, not the thoracic cage measurements shown.

The involved hemithorax is expanded

Tension pneumothorax creates a pleural line with absent peripheral vascular markings and a collapsed central lung, not a multicystic parenchymal lesion.
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia shows intrathoracic bowel loops or stomach and an abnormal diaphragmatic contour rather than this pulmonary multicystic pattern.
